prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

justice: The street allocates very large space to multiple motor-vehicle lanes in the center, while pedestrian space is limited to narrow side sidewalks visible along both edges, suggesting an uneven distribution of street space across user types.

Continuous sidewalks appear to exist on both sides of the road, which supports baseline access for all road users, but no visible marked crosswalks, pedestrian refuge islands, or curb ramps can be confirmed in this view.

Street lighting, planted medians, and roadside greenery are provided along the corridor, indicating some public investment for all users, yet the design visibly prioritizes through-traffic over pedestrian activity or social use.
No dedicated bicycle lane, bus stop, tactile paving, or other clearly inclusive multimodal facilities are visible, so fairness across different travel modes appears limited in the observed segment.
safety: The roadway is wide, straight, and well maintained, with clear dashed lane markings that help organize vehicle movement and reduce immediate lane ambiguity.
A planted median and edge planting strips create physical separation between opposing traffic and between the carriageway and sidewalks, which can reduce some conflict exposure.
Tall streetlights are regularly spaced along the corridor, supporting visibility and perceived safety, especially compared with an unlit arterial road.
However, the long straight alignment and broad lane geometry may encourage higher driving speeds, which can increase crash severity for any crossing pedestrian or roadside user.
No visible pedestrian crossings, traffic calming devices, or protected cycling facilities are present in the image, limiting safety support for non-motorized users.
livability: The corridor appears clean, orderly, and landscaped with trees, shrubs, and medians, which improves environmental quality compared with a bare roadway.

Despite the greenery, the scene shows little active frontage: one side is lined by a long green wall and the other side by setback vegetation, with no visible shops, seating, or community destinations.
There are no visible pedestrians, cyclists, benches, kiosks, or social gathering spaces, so the street functions more like a movement corridor than a lively public place.
The very wide carriageway and sparse human activity reduce the sense of everyday street life and neighborhood interaction.
sustainability: Rows of street trees, shrubs, and planted medians provide some green infrastructure and can contribute modestly to cooling, air-quality improvement, and visual softening.
The landscaped center and roadside planting strips indicate more ecological consideration than a fully paved arterial corridor.
However, the dominant feature remains a wide multi-lane road designed for motor traffic, which suggests a car-oriented mobility pattern rather than strong support for low-carbon travel.
No visible bike lanes, bus lanes, bus stops, or other public-transport facilities can be identified, limiting evidence of sustainable mode prioritization.
The young and relatively sparse tree canopy provides limited immediate shade and ecosystem benefit compared with mature, dense street greenery.
aesthetics: The street has a neat and coherent visual composition, with symmetrical lane layout, consistent streetlights, and continuous planted medians.
Trees and trimmed shrubs on both sides soften the large roadway and improve the visual quality of the corridor.
The pavement appears smooth and well maintained, contributing to an orderly and cared-for appearance.
At the same time, the long green wall on the right and the expansive asphalt surface create a somewhat monotonous visual experience with limited architectural interest or human-scale detail.
comfort: The road surface looks smooth and even, which supports physical comfort for vehicle travel and likely for walking on the visible sidewalks.
Landscaped strips and trees along both sides provide some buffering from traffic and improve psychological comfort compared with an entirely exposed roadway.
Thermal comfort appears only moderate because the trees are young and sparse, casting little visible shade onto the sidewalks or roadway.
No benches, shelters, or resting amenities are visible, so stationary comfort for people outside vehicles is weak.
The broad roadway may also generate noise and speed-related stress for pedestrians, even though the corridor looks uncrowded in this image.
walkability: Sidewalks are visible on both sides of the street, so there is at least basic pedestrian infrastructure and route continuity along the corridor.
However, the sidewalks appear secondary to the very wide carriageway, and there are no visible marked crosswalks, pedestrian signals, or refuge islands to support safe crossing.
The long block form, setback edges, and absence of active storefronts or entrances reduce walking interest and destination appeal.
Limited shade from young trees lowers walking comfort, especially in warm weather, and no benches or shelters are visible for rest.
Overall, the image suggests a road that can be walked along, but not a street strongly designed to invite or prioritize walking.

prompt_c3:
As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

 5. Quality Redlines:
1. All scores must include one decimal place.
2. Each array in explanations must contain at least 3 reasons based on specific objects in the image (e.g., benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings).
3. Analysis content must strictly match the persona setting; generic evaluations unrelated to the specified perspective are strictly prohibited.

For instance, one participant expressed their priorities clearly: “I just want safe and protected bike lanes, safe pedestrian crossings, wider and shaded footpaths, and raised crossings at intersections, so cars have to go over the raised area instead of pedestrians having to go down onto the road” (M, 36). The need for broader changes to address these issues was repeatedly highlighted, as another participant noted: “Footpaths are too narrow and poorly maintained, there are not enough safe crossings with islands, cyclists should always have permanent, dedicated lanes wherever there is a road, and they should really fix the train bridges so there are no at-road level crossings. More pedestrian refuge islands is also a brilliant opportunity to plant more trees” (F, 31). These suggestions underline the interconnected benefits of safety improvements and environmental enhancements. Participants consistently linked infrastructure upgrades to safety and justice, reflecting a belief that physical changes to the transport system are foundational for achieving equity. One participant succinctly summarised this perspective: “The government desperately needs to improve the pedestrian and cyclist safety situations. Footpaths are too narrow and poorly maintained, and there are not enough safe crossings with islands” (F, 33). Another added, “Prioritise infrastructure for vulnerable road users so we don’t have to share with any motor vehicles” (M, 52). Collectively, these responses reflect a strong consensus that redesigning infrastructure is essential for creating a safer and fairer transport system that can effectively integrate CAVs. 3.5.3. Inclusivity and accessibility Codes such as “inclusive design,” “accessible vehicles,” and “no burden on VRUs” reflected participants’ concerns about marginalised groups, particularly people with disabilities, the elderly, and those without access to wearable technology. Concerns around inclusivity and accessibility were prominent, with participants firmly rejecting policies that placed the burden of adaptation on VRUs. Many criticised proposals requiring VRUs to use reflective clothing, specific apps, or wearable devices to ensure their visibility to CAVs. One participant voiced their frustration: “Pedestrians should NOT have to wear something so that these cars can see them… If the robot can’t see pedestrians, then it should not be allowed on the road” (NB, 18).
